Prior stage reviewers (reviewer_1, reviewer_2, reviewer_3) all flagged this as critical gap
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct paired t-tests or bootstrap confidence intervals on accuracy metrics. Report p-values and 95% confidence intervals for all accuracy comparisons. If differences are not statistically significant at p<0.05, revise claims to reflect uncertainty.

concerns.title: Confounded comparison: PMI-IR tested on reduced dataset
concerns.description: PMI-IR baseline is tested on 7,646 reviews (due to pattern matching constraints) while VSM methods are tested on full 9,613 reviews. This confounds the comparison and makes it unfair.
evidence: Authors state: 'the test dataset consists of 7,646 posts out of the 9,613 reviews' for PMI-IR (line 599)
VSM methods evaluated on full 9,613 reviews (line 300)
This 20% dataset size difference is not acknowledged as a confound in results or discussion
Prior stage reviewers (reviewer_1, reviewer_2, reviewer_3, reviewer_4) all identified this as critical confound
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Re-evaluate PMI-IR on the full 9,613 reviews by relaxing pattern matching constraints or using alternative phrase extraction. Alternatively, evaluate all methods on the reduced 7,646-review subset and report both results. Discuss how dataset size affects accuracy estimates.

concerns.title: Weak word-level correlations suggest limited sentiment signal
concerns.description: Word-level correlations with gold-standard annotations are modest (0.25–0.33 Pearson), suggesting the discovered sentiment dimensions capture only weak signal. Unclear if this translates to meaningful classification performance.
evidence: Table 2 reports: Word2Vec (size 3) 0.33 Pearson, GloVe (size 3) 0.28 Pearson
All correlations in 0.25–0.33 range across models and context window sizes
Figure 2 visualization shows substantial overlap between red (positive) and blue (negative) clusters, indicating imperfect separation
Authors do not discuss whether 0.25–0.33 correlation is sufficient for downstream tasks
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Analyze the relationship between word-level correlation strength and review-level classification accuracy. Conduct error analysis to identify which words are misclassified and why. Compare correlation magnitudes with other sentiment lexicons (e.g., SentiWordNet) to contextualize the weakness.

concerns.title: Confounded model comparison: different context window sizes for Word2Vec vs. GloVe
concerns.description: Word2Vec is evaluated with context window size 3, while GloVe is evaluated with size 10. This hyperparameter difference confounds the comparison and makes it unclear whether performance differences reflect model architecture or hyperparameter choices.
evidence: Authors state: 'We set the context window size to 3 for the Word2Vec (Skip-gram based) and 10 for the GloVe model' (line 500)
Table 2 shows Word2Vec performance degrades with larger context windows (0.33 at size 3 → 0.25 at size 10)
GloVe remains stable across context window sizes (0.28–0.28), suggesting different sensitivity to hyperparameters
Authors do not justify why different window sizes were chosen or acknowledge this as a confound
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate both Word2Vec and GloVe with the same context window sizes (e.g., 3, 5, 7, 10). Report results in a table showing performance across window sizes for both models. Discuss whether performance differences are due to model architecture or hyperparameter sensitivity.

concerns.title: Claim about 'denser vector spaces' for Word2Vec is unsupported
concerns.description: Authors assert that Word2Vec produces 'denser vector spaces' than GloVe, but provide no empirical evidence (e.g., sparsity metrics, proportion of zero elements, L0 norm). This claim is central to the paradigmatic vs. collocational argument but remains unvalidated.
evidence: Authors state: 'Skip-grams essentially exploit paradigmatic relations between words and produce denser vector spaces' (line 673)
No sparsity metrics reported anywhere in paper
No comparison of vector density, zero-element proportions, or other sparsity measures between Word2Vec and GloVe
Prior stage reviewers (reviewer_1, reviewer_2, reviewer_4) all flagged this as unsupported claim
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Compute and report sparsity metrics for Word2Vec and GloVe embeddings (e.g., proportion of zero elements, L0 norm, average non-zero magnitude). Create visualizations comparing vector density distributions. If Word2Vec is not actually denser, revise the theoretical explanation for performance differences.

concerns.title: PCA dimensionality choice (2D) is not justified
concerns.description: Authors fix PCA projection to 2 dimensions without justification or comparison with other dimensionality choices. Unclear if 2D is optimal or arbitrary.
evidence: Authors state: 'In the analysis, we only use the value of two for the number of dimensions to project the entities into the reduced space' (line 350–400)
No explanation for why 2D was chosen
No comparison with 1D, 3D, 5D, or other dimensionality choices
No analysis of variance explained by first two principal components
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Report variance explained by each principal component. Evaluate classification accuracy with different dimensionality choices (1D, 2D, 3D, 5D, 10D). Create a plot showing accuracy vs. dimensionality. Justify the choice of 2D based on empirical results.

concerns.title: Vector averaging for reference vector construction is acknowledged as suboptimal
concerns.description: Authors explicitly acknowledge that vector averaging is 'not efficient for the purpose in this research' (lines 673–683) but do not explore alternative methods. This leaves the method in a suboptimal state.
evidence: Authors state: 'the type of vector calculation is not efficient for the purpose in this research' (lines 673–683)
No comparison with alternative reference vector construction methods (weighted averaging, centroid optimization, learned projections)
Performance plateau with increasing point words (Figure 2) suggests averaging does not scale well
Authors identify this as a limitation but do not address it
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Explore alternative reference vector construction methods: (1) weighted averaging based on correlation strength, (2) centroid optimization via gradient descent, (3) learned projection matrices. Report accuracy improvements for each method. Discuss why averaging is suboptimal and how alternatives address this.

concerns.title: Practical advantages over PMI-IR are asserted but not quantified
concerns.description: Authors claim the method is 'more practical and data efficient' than PMI-IR but provide no quantitative comparison of computational cost, query latency, memory requirements, or reproducibility.
evidence: Abstract claims method is 'more practical and data efficient' (line 099)
Discussion states: 'It is worth noting that PMI-IR suffers from data-deficiency' (lines 673–683)
No computational cost comparison (embedding training time vs. search engine queries)
No query latency analysis or memory requirements comparison
No discussion of Yandex API reliability or long-term reproducibility
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Quantify practical advantages: (1) measure embedding training time and memory requirements, (2) measure PMI-IR query time and API latency, (3) compare total computational cost, (4) discuss reproducibility and long-term API availability. Create a table comparing practical metrics.

concerns.title: Paradigmatic vs. collocational distinction is asserted but not empirically validated
concerns.description: The core theoretical claim that paradigmatic relations (Word2Vec) are superior to collocational relations (GloVe, PMI-IR) for sentiment discovery is asserted but not rigorously tested. Different context windows and modest performance differences confound the comparison.
evidence: Authors argue: 'Skip-grams essentially exploit paradigmatic relations between words and produce denser vector spaces' (line 673)
Word2Vec outperforms GloVe by only 3–4 percentage points (Table 3, line 599)
Different context window sizes (3 vs. 10) confound the comparison (line 500)
GloVe correlation remains stable across context window sizes (Table 2), contradicting the paradigmatic vs. collocational hypothesis
No direct test of whether paradigmatic relations are actually more informative for sentiment
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Design a controlled experiment: (1) evaluate Word2Vec and GloVe with identical context window sizes, (2) analyze which types of word relations (paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic) are most predictive of sentiment, (3) conduct ablation studies removing paradigmatic or syntagmatic information and measuring impact on accuracy. Provide direct evidence for the theoretical claim.

concerns.title: Cross-domain generalizability of semi-supervised method is not validated
concerns.description: Semi-supervised method uses IMDB movie review polarity labels as weak labels. Unclear if this approach generalizes to other domains (e.g., product reviews, news articles). Authors do not test cross-domain applicability.
evidence: Semi-supervised method relies on IMDB polarity ratings (line 350)
Authors claim: 'adjectives and adverbs are generally used with their own static stance' and can be applied to unseen texts (line 350)
No cross-domain evaluation provided; only tested on Stanford Sentiment Treebank (movie reviews)
No discussion of domain-specific polarity variations
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Evaluate semi-supervised method on out-of-domain datasets (e.g., product reviews, news articles, social media). Compare accuracy with in-domain (movie review) performance. Analyze which words have domain-specific polarity shifts. Discuss generalizability limitations.

concerns.title: Hyperparameter selection appears ad-hoc without systematic justification
concerns.description: Context window sizes, frequency cutoffs, embedding dimensionality, and PCA dimensionality are chosen without principled justification or systematic optimization. Results may be sensitive to these choices.

Embedding dimensionality fixed at 100 (line 500) without comparison with other choices
PCA dimensionality fixed at 2 without justification (line 350–400)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct systematic hyperparameter optimization: (1) grid search over context window sizes (3, 5, 7, 10) for both models, (2) grid search over frequency cutoffs, (3) grid search over embedding dimensionality (50, 100, 200, 300), (4) grid search over PCA dimensionality (1, 2, 3, 5, 10). Report results in a table or heatmap. Justify final hyperparameter choices based on validation performance.

concerns.title: Variance metric in Figure 1 is not clearly defined
concerns.description: Figure 1 shows 'Variances of polarity values per POS-tags' but the variance metric is not clearly defined. Unclear if this is variance of polarity ratings or variance of word frequency.
evidence: Figure 1 caption states: 'Variances of polarity values per POS-tags' (line 350)
No definition of variance metric provided in methods or figure caption
Unclear if variance is computed across words (variance of polarity ratings for words with given POS tag) or across instances (variance of polarity ratings for word instances)
concerns.actionable_suggestion: Clarify the variance metric in Figure 1 caption. Provide formula or definition. Explain whether variance is computed across word types or word instances. Discuss what high variance means for sentiment discovery (signal vs. noise).

concerns.title: No ablation study comparing performance with other POS tag selections
concerns.description: Authors select adjectives and adverbs as point words based on variance analysis, but do not conduct ablation studies comparing performance with other POS tag selections or combinations.
evidence: Authors justify adjective/adverb selection via Figure 1 variance analysis (line 350)
No ablation study comparing performance with: (1) all POS tags, (2) only adjectives, (3) only adverbs, (4) adjectives + adverbs + verbs, etc.

concerns.actionable_suggestion: Conduct ablation studies: (1) evaluate with all POS tags, (2) evaluate with only adjectives, (3) evaluate with only adverbs, (4) evaluate with adjectives + adverbs + verbs. Report accuracy for each variant. Discuss whether adjectives/adverbs are uniquely informative or if other POS tags contribute.

concerns.title: Novelty claim is overstated; contribution is incremental

concerns.title: Sparse precedent in retrieved literature may reflect indexing gaps rather than genuine novelty

Search for: (1) dimensionality reduction applied to sentiment analysis, (2) PCA applied to word embeddings, (3) sentiment dimension discovery in vector spaces. Cite relevant prior work if found. uncertainty_flags: Statistical significance of accuracy differences (3–9 percentage points) is not reported; improvements may be within noise margins or due to random variation
Modest word-level correlations (0.25–0.33) suggest weak alignment between discovered dimensions and gold-standard annotations; unclear if sufficient for reliable sentiment discovery
PCA visualization (Figure 2) shows substantial overlap between positive and negative clusters, indicating imperfect separation and potential noise in discovered dimensions
PMI-IR baseline tested on reduced dataset (7,646 reviews) vs. full dataset (9,613 reviews) due to pattern matching constraints; confounds direct comparison and makes PMI-IR appear weaker than it is
Vector averaging for reference vector construction is acknowledged as suboptimal; performance may improve substantially with better reference vector construction methods
Hyperparameter selection (context window, frequency cutoff, embedding dimensionality, PCA dimensionality) appears ad-hoc; results may be sensitive to these choices
Cross-domain generalizability of semi-supervised method not validated; IMDB polarity labels may be domain-specific and not transfer to other domains
Claim about 'denser vector spaces' for Word2Vec not empirically demonstrated; no sparsity metrics provided to support this assertion
Choice of 2D PCA projection not justified; unclear if 2D is optimal or arbitrary; no comparison with other dimensionality choices
Assumption that word polarity is 'static' across domains unvalidated; word sentiment may vary by context and domain
Different context window sizes for Word2Vec (3) vs. GloVe (10) confound model comparison; unclear if performance differences reflect model architecture or hyperparameter choices
Seed word choice ('excellent', 'poor') not validated; no sensitivity analysis for alternative seed words
Pattern extraction rules (Table 1) may miss sentiment-bearing phrases or include non-sentiment phrases; no precision/recall analysis provided
Variance metric in Figure 1 not clearly defined; unclear if this is variance of polarity ratings or variance of word frequency
alternative_interpretations: Word2Vec outperforms GloVe not because of paradigmatic vs. collocational relations, but because of hyperparameter choices (context window 3 vs. 10). A fair comparison with identical hyperparameters might show no significant difference.

Modest improvements over PMI-IR (4 percentage points) may reflect the reduced dataset size for PMI-IR (7,646 vs. 9,613 reviews) rather than fundamental superiority of dense embeddings. Fair comparison on same dataset might show smaller or no difference.

Weak word-level correlations (0.25–0.33) suggest the discovered sentiment dimensions capture noise rather than signal. The modest review-level classification improvements may be due to other factors (e.g., word frequency, document length) rather than sentiment orientation.

Vector averaging for reference vector construction may be the bottleneck limiting performance. Alternative reference vector construction methods might yield substantially larger improvements, making the comparison with PMI-IR less favorable.

The paradigmatic vs. collocational distinction may not be the primary driver of performance differences. Other factors (embedding training procedure, corpus size, hyperparameters) may be more important.

Semi-supervised improvements (4–5 percentage points) may reflect the additional information from IMDB labels rather than the superiority of the method. A fair comparison would use external labels for PMI-IR as well.

The method may not be more 'practical' than PMI-IR in absolute terms. Embedding training is computationally expensive; PMI-IR queries may be faster in some scenarios. Quantitative comparison is needed.

The claim about 'data efficiency' may be misleading. The method requires 50,000 reviews for embedding training; PMI-IR requires search engine queries. Total data/computational requirements may be comparable or favor PMI-IR.

PCA may not be discovering a meaningful sentiment dimension. The modest correlations and visual overlap in Figure 2 suggest PCA is extracting noise or spurious patterns rather than genuine sentiment structure.
transparency_notes: This review prioritizes evidence-based assessment of claims over binary verdicts. All claims are cross-checked against manuscript evidence and prior work.
Uncertainty flags are explicitly separated from confirmed findings. Confidence levels reflect the strength of evidence, not the reviewer's subjective judgment.
Alternative interpretations are provided to acknowledge that the data can be read in multiple ways. The paper's conclusions are not the only valid interpretation of the results.
Novelty assessment is separated from validity assessment. Sparse precedent in the retrieved literature corpus does not validate novelty; it may reflect indexing gaps.
Methodological flaws are distinguished from novelty risks. A paper can be methodologically flawed but novel, or methodologically sound but incremental.
The review acknowledges limitations of the retrieved literature corpus. Absence of a close match does not imply invalidity; it may reflect conceptual divergence or sparse coverage.
Prior stage digests are used as common reviewer memory. This review builds on and extends the analysis from structure, methodology, and novelty reviewers.
Actionable suggestions are provided for each concern, enabling authors to address issues in revision.
Confidence intervals are provided for the overall assessment, reflecting uncertainty about the paper's contributions and limitations.

The novelty is in the combination and application rather than in fundamental methodological innovation.

confidence_interval.rationale: The paper presents a methodologically sound but empirically modest contribution with significant gaps between claims and evidence. The lower bound (0.35) reflects major concerns: lack of statistical significance testing, confounded comparisons, weak word-level correlations, and unvalidated theoretical claims. The upper bound (0.65) reflects strengths: clear motivation, comprehensive ablation studies, direct baseline replication, and acknowledgment of limitations. The wide interval (0.30) reflects high uncertainty due to missing statistical tests, confounded experimental design, and alternative interpretations of results. The paper could be strengthened substantially by addressing methodological flaws and providing rigorous statistical validation. Novelty is incremental but not invalid; the conceptual framing of sentiment discovery as dimensionality reduction is interesting but not sufficiently validated empirically.

consensus_findings: The paper proposes a PCA-based vector space model (VSM) approach for discovering sentiment dimensions in word embeddings (Word2Vec, GloVe) and measuring word-level sentiment orientation. Core claims: (1) dense vector models outperform collocation-based PMI-IR; (2) Word2Vec Skip-gram (paradigmatic) outperforms GloVe (collocational); (3) semi-supervised variants using IMDB labels improve unsupervised performance; (4) the method is more practical and data-efficient than PMI-IR.

Empirical results show modest accuracy improvements: Word2Vec unsupervised 61% vs. PMI-IR 57% (4 percentage points); Word2Vec semi-supervised 66% vs. GloVe semi-supervised 63% (3 percentage points). Word-level correlations with gold-standard annotations are weak: 0.25–0.33 Pearson for both Word2Vec and GloVe.

The paper is well-motivated theoretically, grounding the work in distributional hypothesis, paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic relations, and conceptual spaces theory. The experimental design includes systematic ablation studies (unsupervised vs. semi-supervised, Word2Vec vs. GloVe, hyperparameter sensitivity).

All five specialist reviewers identified critical methodological gaps: (1) lack of statistical significance testing for accuracy differences; (2) confounded comparison with PMI-IR tested on reduced dataset (7,646 reviews) vs. VSM methods on full dataset (9,613 reviews); (3) different context window sizes for Word2Vec (3) vs. GloVe (10), confounding model comparison; (4) weak word-level correlations (0.25–0.33) suggesting limited sentiment signal; (5) unvalidated claims about 'denser vector spaces' for Word2Vec.

The paper acknowledges several limitations: vector averaging for reference vector construction is 'not efficient' (lines 673–683); performance plateaus with increasing point words; authors identify potential improvements but do not implement them.

Novelty assessment is mixed: the conceptual framing of sentiment discovery as dimensionality reduction in embedding spaces lacks close analogs in the retrieved literature (potential innovation signal), but the execution relies on straightforward application of existing techniques (PCA, Word2Vec, GloVe, cosine distance) without significant algorithmic innovation.

Practical advantages over PMI-IR are asserted (50K corpus vs. 350M pages, no search engine dependency) but not quantified. No computational cost comparison, query latency analysis, or reproducibility assessment provided.

The paper's contribution is methodologically sound but empirically modest. The work makes a reasonable contribution to sentiment analysis methodology but lacks the rigor and innovation depth expected for high-impact venues.
disagreements: Interpretation of novelty: Structure analyst (reviewer_1) emphasizes limited novelty of combining existing techniques; methodology auditor (reviewer_2) focuses on methodological flaws regardless of novelty; incremental assessor (reviewer_3) treats contribution as incremental but reasonable; disruptive assessor (reviewer_4) identifies conceptual novelty in dimensionality-reduction framing but notes unvalidated claims; claim verifier (reviewer_5) separates novelty from validity and treats sparse precedent as potential innovation signal. Consensus: novelty is incremental with some conceptual interest but insufficient empirical validation.

Severity of confounded comparison (PMI-IR on reduced dataset): All reviewers flag this as a major methodological flaw, but differ in emphasis. Structure analyst and methodology auditor treat it as critical; incremental assessor notes it but focuses on other gaps; disruptive assessor emphasizes it as undermining practical advantage claims; claim verifier treats it as confounding the entire comparison. Baseline implementation: The PMI-IR baseline uses Yandex search engine (2017) rather than the original AltaVista (2002). Comparability to Turney's original work is unclear. Different search engines may have different indexing and policies.

Literature coverage: The retrieved literature corpus may have indexing gaps, affecting assessment of novelty and precedent. Sparse precedent may reflect coverage limitations rather than genuine novelty.

- Paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic distinction is asserted but not empirically validated: Central theoretical claim lacks rigorous testing. Different context windows confound the comparison. GloVe's stable correlation across window sizes contradicts the hypothesis that paradigmatic relations are superior. No ablation study isolates paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic effects.

Open Questions:
- Are the accuracy improvements (4–9 percentage points) statistically significant? What are the 95% confidence intervals? Conducting bootstrap resampling or permutation tests would clarify whether observed differences are meaningful or within noise margins. This is essential for validating the main empirical claim.
- How would results change if PMI-IR and VSM methods were evaluated on the same dataset (either 7,646 or 9,613 reviews)? The current confounded comparison makes it impossible to fairly assess relative method performance. Re-evaluation on matched datasets is critical.
- Do Word2Vec and GloVe actually differ in paradigmatic vs. syntagmatic properties, or are performance differences due to hyperparameter choices? Fair comparison requires identical context window sizes. Why does GloVe correlation remain stable across window sizes if collocational models suffer from data sparsity?
- What is the relationship between weak word-level correlations (0.25–0.33) and review-level classification accuracy? Do weak word-level signals translate to meaningful classification performance? Error analysis identifying misclassified words would clarify this.
- How does the semi-supervised method generalize to out-of-domain data (product reviews, news, social media)? Is the assumption that word polarity is 'static' across domains actually valid? Cross-domain evaluation is essential for assessing practical applicability.

Transparency:
Five specialist reviewers with different cognitive roles and epistemic variants were employed to provide diverse perspectives. All reviewers had access to shared extraction stage and comparable works from literature retrieval. Consensus findings reflect areas of strong agreement: methodological gaps (lack of significance testing, confounded comparisons), weak empirical evidence (modest correlations, small accuracy improvements), and unvalidated theoretical claims. Disagreements are primarily on emphasis and interpretation rather than factual assessment. Uncertainty hotspots reflect areas where reviewers acknowledge genuine uncertainty: statistical significance of improvements, interpretation of weak correlations, validity of theoretical claims, and practical advantages of the method. Epistemic transparency: This meta-review prioritizes evidence-based assessment over binary verdicts. Claims are cross-checked against manuscript evidence and prior work. Alternative interpretations are provided to acknowledge that data can be read in multiple ways. Confidence intervals reflect uncertainty rather than false precision. Limitations of assessment: Retrieved literature corpus may have indexing gaps affecting novelty assessment. Specialist reviewers did not have access to author responses or revisions. Statistical power analysis was not conducted. No direct access to raw data or code to verify computational results.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.title: Document 2
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

top_documents.title: Document 2
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Codes: none

Content: n doubt, consider the scope described in ARR CFP and any relevant conferences (e.g. for October 2024 cycle the NAACL CFP specifies the special theme “NLP in a Multicultural World”. Hallucinated references or citations: Please check carefully for hallucinated references, which pose a serious concern to scientific reliability. Anonymity violations. As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link). Style guides or length violations: the paper should be desk-rejected if it does not follow the style guides or goes over the page limit (4 pages for short, 8 for long papers, excluding the ethical considerations and limitations).

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

top_documents.title: Document 4
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

top_documents.title: Document 3
top_documents.abstract_or_snippet:
Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Section: Q: Why is peer review so inconsistent?
Codes: none
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: much attention. In case of submissions that get deanonymized due to preprints and social media, we may also be biased in favor of well-known authors and/or widely-discussed papers. These guidelines are a part of an effort to improve the overall quality of reviews at *CL conferences, aiming to address the above issues. We discuss the overall structure and philosophy of the process for first-time reviewers, clarify the ARR principles and the review form, and address some of the cognitive and social biases that undermine peer review. Note that reviewer guidelines address only the variance in the review process, not the acceptance decisions. Top-tier conferences usually have more high-quality submissions that receive good reviews than they can accept, and then the decisions are also motivated by space and quota constraints, and editorial priorities of the chairs. 🆕 See sec. 7 of ACL’23 report for analysis of the effect of reviews, meta-reviews, and SAC recommendations on the final decision.

Guideline Document: ARR Reviewer Guidelines
Section: 6. Check that the tone is professional and neutral I4
Codes: I4
Applies To: meta_reviewer
Content: Above all, a good review should be professional and neutral, if not kind. A key goal of peer review is to help the authors improve their papers. As an anonymous reviewer, you are in a position of power, and the written medium makes it easier to be more dismissive and sarcastic than if you were communicating with the authors face-to-face. Unfortunately such reviews are not uncommon. Consider that you may well be addressing someone who is only starting on the research path. And/or someone struggling with stress and other mental health issues. And/or someone who has been less lucky with their school and advisors. Academic lives are already stressful enough, and we do not need to inflict extra damage on the mental health of our colleagues with sarcastic or insulting reviews. Write the review you would like to get yourself. The fact is, authors and reviewers are actually the same people: the conference crowd lining up for coffee, happily chatting with each other about the grand problems even if they do not always agree. Why can’t we do peer review in the same spirit of fun intellectual interaction with colleagues? Just like the conference coffee break chats, reviewing is in fact, mutually beneficial: in exchange for feedback, the reviewers get to have the first look at cutting-edge research. Just like the coffee breaks, where you do not necessarily meet only the people working in your subsubfield, peer review may expose you to new techniques.

As of January 2024, non-anonymous pre-prints are permitted for ARR, but submissions should still be properly anonymized (e.g., not containing explicit references to the authors’ prior work, acknowledgements, links to non-anonymous repositories or services like Dropbox that may track who opened the link).
